hints.content:
Usually, there are many different ways to divide polynomials. Here, we will use the method of splitting the quotient into multiple quotients:

$\dfrac{4x^3-3x+1}{x}=\dfrac{4x^3}{x}-\dfrac{3x}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x}$

Now let's try to cancel common factors in the resulting terms.

$\begin{align}
\dfrac{4x^3}{x}&=4x^2
\\\\
-\dfrac{3x}{x}&=-3
\end{align}$

$\dfrac{1}{x}$ doesn't have common factors so it has to stay as it is.

In conclusion, this is the result of dividing the polynomials:

$4x^2-3+\dfrac{1}{x}$

[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
We can perform the division using polynomial long division. Notice the numerator is missing a $2^{\text{nd}}$ degree term. Let's add it as $0x^2$:

$\begin{array}{r}
4x^2+0x-3
\\
x|\overline{4x^3+0x^2-3x+1}
\\
\mathllap{-(}\underline{4x^3\phantom{+0x^2-3x+1}\rlap )}
\\
0x^2-3x+1
\\
\mathllap{-(}\underline{0x^2\phantom{-3x+1}\rlap )}
\\
{}-3x+1
\\
\mathllap{-(}\underline{{}-3x\phantom{-2}\rlap )}
\\
1
\end{array}$

We get that the quotient is $4x^2-3$ and the remainder is $1$, and therefore:

$\dfrac{4x^3-3x+1}{x}=4x^2-3+\dfrac{1}{x}$
